Early life history stages in Catla (Labeo catla) begin with the fertilised ovum, which develops rapidly under local pond conditions. At a water temperature of 28 °C [T = 28 °C], the yolk-sac larva emerges via chorion rupture after approximately 2 days [ab = approximately 2 days], marking a brief endotrophic period. The newly emerged prolarva, still dependent on endogenous yolk reserves, weighs a mere 0.0005236 grams [Wwb = 0.0005236 grams], reflecting the small egg size typical of many cyprinids. This lecithotrophic phase is short, and the onset of exogenous feeding occurs quickly as the mouth opens and retinal differentiation allows first prey capture. During the pelagic larval phase, growth is rapid and driven by abundant zooplankton in tropical nursery grounds. Field records indicate that under optimal thermal regimes, the larval-juvenile transition is completed within a few weeks, after which the fingerlings recruit to coastal feeding areas. The extreme fecundity of this species is well documented; at 28 °C [T = 28 °C], a single gravid fish can produce approximately 9,863 eggs per day across a spawning season [Ri = approximately 9,863 eggs per day across a spawning season], reflecting an enormous clutch output that compensates for high early-stage mortality observed in riverine habitats.

Body size parameters in Catla are substantial, with mature adults reaching considerable dimensions. The ultimate total length recorded for this species is 182 cm [Li = 182 cm], placing it among the largest of the Indian major carps. This asymptotic length is attained after a prolonged growth period, and individuals in productive reservoirs regularly exceed 150 cm. The wet weight at puberty for females, a critical demographic threshold, occurs at 2,000 grams [Wwp = 2,000 grams], a body mass that signals the onset of reproductive competence. This mass is reached relatively early considering the species' large ultimate size, and it correlates with the attainment of a specific total length at puberty for females of 67.8 cm [Lp = 67.8 cm]. This length was calculated from the relationship between mass at puberty and ultimate mass relative to maximum length, and it serves as a reliable field metric for assessing reproductive readiness in wild stocks. Comparative studies with other cyprinids suggest that Catla achieves this maturity size at a younger age than related species of equivalent asymptotic mass, a pattern linked to its planktivorous feeding strategy that supports high somatic growth rates during the juvenile phase.

Reproductive investment in Catla is characterised by extreme fecundity paired with a compressed spawning window. Under stable thermal regimes of 28 °C [T = 28 °C], a single female releases roughly 9,863 eggs per day [Ri = roughly 9,863 eggs per day] over the duration of the monsoon breeding period. This daily output, sustained for several weeks, constitutes the maximum reproduction rate for the species. The reproductive frequency is approximately one spawning event per year [F_R_i = approximately one spawning event per year], timed to coincide with river flooding that facilitates egg dispersion and larval drift. The enormous daily egg production is an adaptive response to high predation pressure on ichthyoplankton in turbid floodplain habitats. Ultra-fine, demersal eggs are broadcast into the water column during a synchronised spawning event that involves multiple adults, enhancing fertilisation success. Female condition factor declines markedly after spawning, indicating that the energetic cost of producing such vast quantities of yolk-laden ova is substantial. Gonadal recrudescence begins shortly after the post-monsoon period, with vitellogenesis onset driven by rising temperatures and increasing photoperiod.

Age-related life history parameters for Catla have been estimated from mark-recapture studies and otolith annuli analysis. At a temperature of 28 °C [T = 28 °C], the emergence of the yolk-sac larva occurs at an age at birth of 2 days [ab = 2 days], a value consistent with the rapid embryonic development seen in other tropical cyprinids. The transition to the exotrophic larval stage follows quickly, and juvenile growth proceeds without an overwintering pause, given the stable thermal environment. Sexual maturation occurs relatively early in the life cycle; captive-reared females attain puberty at 2 years [tp = 2 years] when maintained at 28 °C [T = 28 °C], though wild fish in less productive systems may experience a slight delay. This age at puberty for females of 730 days [tp = 730 days] is modest compared to the species' overall lifespan at a temperature of 28 °C [T = 28 °C]. The maximum recorded longevity for Catla in natural populations is 10 years [am = 10 years] at 28 °C [T = 28 °C], corresponding to approximately 3,650 days [am = approximately 3,650 days]. Senescent individuals exhibit reduced feeding activity and a decline in gonadosomatic index, with natural mortality typically observed during the post-spawning period when body condition is at its lowest.

The ultimate wet weight attained by Catla is 38,600 grams [Wwi = 38,600 grams], a massive body size that makes it the heaviest of the Indian major carps. This asymptotic mass is achieved after a decade of sustained growth in productive lacustrine environments. In contrast, the wet weight at puberty for females is attained at a much earlier stage, with individuals reaching 2,000 grams [Wwp = 2,000 grams] during their second year of life. The ratio between pubertal mass and ultimate mass is approximately 0.052, a relatively low value that indicates a long period of post-pubertal somatic growth before asymptotic size is reached. This pattern is ecologically significant: by becoming reproductively active at a relatively small size, Catla populations can sustain high reproductive output over many years despite individual growth continuing. The ultimate total length of 182 cm [Li = 182 cm] is achieved concurrently with asymptotic mass, with large adults dominating the upper reaches of the water column in deep reservoirs. Total length at puberty for females, measured at 67.8 cm [Lp = 67.8 cm], represents a useful management criterion for setting minimum mesh sizes in gillnet fisheries to protect immature individuals.
